title: What Is the Next Trial Worth? — Raiffa & Schlaifer Expected Value of Sample Information (EVSI), Claxton–Posnett Optimal Trial Sizing & Li Bayesian Value-of-Information Analysis in Kenyan HIV Alcohol Care

teenKit.tldr: In 15 seconds: Before spending millions on another clinical trial, how much could new data actually change the medical decision? Expected Value of Sample Information (EVSI) prices a proposed study by asking how often—and by how much—a finite sample would overturn today's best choice.
teenKit.whyItMatters: P-values never tell you whether a 500-patient trial is too small to matter or wastefully oversized; Bayesian Value of Information weighs health gains directly against trial cost and delay.
keyTakeaways: EVPI (Expected Value of Perfect Information) sets an upper ceiling on research value by asking what eliminating all uncertainty would gain.
EVSI (Raiffa & Schlaifer) simulates realistic noisy trials of size n, updates the posterior each time, and averages the net benefit improvement over choosing today.
Optimal sample size sits where the Expected Net Benefit of Sampling (ENBS = population EVSI minus trial cost) peaks.

vocab.meaning: Expected Value of Perfect Information—the average gain from knowing true parameters with zero error before deciding.
Expected Value of Sample Information—the expected decision gain from running a real study of finite sample size n.
Expected Net Benefit of Sampling: population-scaled EVSI minus the financial and opportunity cost of conducting the trial.

quiz.question: When is the Expected Value of Sample Information (EVSI) equal to zero even if parameter uncertainty remains?
options: When no plausible outcome of the proposed sample could shift the posterior enough to change which treatment maximizes expected net benefit
Whenever a prior distribution is normal
quiz.explanation: Information only has decision value if observing the sample can change the action you take.
